issues.description: A z-value of 0.60 cannot correspond to p < 0.01 (it corresponds to roughly p = 0.55). Either the z, the p, or both are misreported, which undermines confidence in the token-based specificity analysis that is used to argue that behaviour mirrors corpus statistics.
issues.quote: the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: 154 total suffixes minus 64 excluded should leave 90, not 95. This arithmetic error means one of the reported counts (154, 64, or 95) is wrong, casting doubt on the robustness check that the high diagnosticity/specificity values are not driven by rare suffixes.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993).  For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: The go-past time estimate and t-value reported in the text (B = 41, t = 3.837) do not match the values in Table 5 (B = 43, t = 3.76). Similar discrepancies appear for regressions-out (text B = 0.3, z = 3.12 vs. Table B = 0.25, z = 2.65). These inconsistencies between the narrative and the summary table prevent the reader from knowing which values are correct.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) such that go-past times were longer for incongruent trials than for congruent ones.

issues.description: Accuracy reported as '0.86%' (and a range of 0.66%–0.98%) is internally inconsistent: either these are proportions (0.86) mislabeled as percentages, or the comprehension performance was near zero. This reporting error obscures whether participants were actually engaged with the task.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: The abstract, title, and framing repeatedly invoke 'meaning' and 'spelling-to-meaning regularities,' but the entire empirical program operationalizes meaning solely as lexical category (noun/adjective/verb). Lexical category is a narrow grammatical property, not semantic meaning; the broad 'meaning' framing overstates the construct that was actually measured.
issues.quote: we know little about the relationship between spelling and meaning in alphabetic writing systems. We present a computational analysis of English writing in which we develop new constructs to describe this relationship.

issues.subcategory: teleological/functional causal claim from diachronic correlation
issues.description: The central thesis—that English spelling 'became fractionated' so as to 'maximise' transmission of meaningful information—attributes purpose/optimization to a historical process on the basis of correlational diachronic observations. No mechanism or test of the optimization claim is provided, making this an unwarranted teleological causal inference.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.description: The claim that 'the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues... without explicit instruction' and that these cues 'facilitate access to meaning' goes beyond the data. The studies are cross-sectional snapshots of adult performance; no learning was measured, instructional history was not assessed, and 'access to meaning' was never operationalized (only category classification and reading times were measured).
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.description: The conclusion that results were 'unambiguous' and that readers are 'highly sensitive' overstates the evidence. In Experiment 3, congruency had no effect on skipping, first-fixation duration, first-run dwell time, or regressions-in; effects appeared only on two late measures and were modest. Describing the overall pattern as unambiguous misrepresents the partial and stage-specific nature of the findings.
issues.quote: Results of these investigations were unambiguous.  Across three experiments using different paradigms, we found that these regularities impacted on the reading, spelling, and decision-making behaviour of skilled readers.

issues.description: The key claim that spelling conveys more category information than sound rests on a difference in mean entropy of only 0.02 (0.61 vs 0.63) and a slope of 0.9 'significantly different from 1.' This statistically significant but minuscule difference is presented as strong support for the central hypothesis, and elsewhere the suffix analyses are said to 'demonstrate definitively.' The effect size does not justify the strength of the conclusion.
issues.quote: the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.description: All models include only random intercepts for subjects and suffixes, with no random slopes for the within-subject manipulation (condition/congruency) and no random intercept for individual nonword items (which are nested within suffix). Omitting random slopes for within-subject factors is known to inflate Type I error, and ignoring item-level variance may further bias the standard errors of the key effects.
issues.quote: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes.

issues.description: Six eye-movement measures were analyzed for congruency effects with no correction for multiple comparisons, and the authors explicitly note they had 'no concrete predictions' about which measures would be affected. With two of six measures significant, the family-wise error rate is uncontrolled and the selective emphasis on significant late measures raises a forking-paths concern.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: The absence of congruency effects on early measures is interpreted as theoretically meaningful (category information matters only after initial lexical processing). Given the small sample (47), simplified random-effects structure, and the use of nonwords, these nulls may reflect low power rather than a true absence of early effects; accepting the null is not justified without an equivalence test or power analysis.
issues.quote: These results therefore indicate that the category information becomes important following initial lexical processing, when the reader has enough contextual information to understand the sentence and detect any incongruences.

issues.description: Experiment 1 included no non-suffixed (non-pseudoaffixed) control nonwords, so it cannot distinguish whether classification was driven by morphological suffix knowledge or by low-level orthographic regularities at word endings. The authors' stated rationale does not eliminate this confound; it merely declines to address it, yet the results are interpreted as evidence of morphological sensitivity.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.description: Experiment 1 was run at the end of an unspecified longer, unrelated session. The nature of the preceding task is not reported, raising concerns about fatigue, carry-over, or contamination effects that could affect a brief noun/adjective decision task; readers cannot evaluate or replicate these conditions.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.description: In Experiment 2, target vs. non-target spellings were extracted manually, but there is no report of blinding to condition or of inter-rater reliability. Because the dependent variable (whether the produced spelling matched the target) requires judgment and the coder could be aware of the congruent/incongruent context, this introduces potential bias into the key outcome.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points).

issues.description: All three experiments used small samples of Royal Holloway undergraduates (n = 46, 29, 47) with no power analysis, yet conclusions are generalized to 'skilled readers' broadly. The narrow demographic (young, highly educated, native English) limits generalizability, and the small samples are particularly concerning for the graded/interaction analyses on suffix subsets.
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.  Sampling conditions were otherwise the same as in Experiment 1.

issues.description: The authors assert that diagnosticity and specificity reflect 'general cognitive principles' that 'must manifest' in other orthographies, despite having studied only English. This is an unsupported extrapolation from a single writing system, especially given their own argument that English evolved under uniquely 'minimal environmental constraints.'
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc exclusions / undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The 'Why are some suffixes more diagnostic' analyses involve numerous post-hoc exclusions (removing 7 suffixes below 0.35, then all 40 with diagnosticity = 1; removing 20 or 29 low-specificity suffixes; removing all specificity = 1 suffixes) with category-based justifications applied after seeing the data. Reversing the sign of a correlation (from -0.24 to +0.23) by removing a subset of cases is a clear instance of analytic flexibility that was not pre-registered.
issues.quote: Surprisingly, the correlation was negative, i.e. -0.24, p < 0.01, but this was entirely due to suffixes with diagnosticity of 1... Once we remove these 40 suffixes, a positive correlation is observed (0.23, p < 0.05)

issues.description: In Experiment 1, 11.7% of data points were discarded due to timeouts or invalid responses, but there is no analysis of whether missingness differed by condition (e.g., whether harder/less diagnostic items timed out more often). Non-random missingness tied to the manipulation could bias the estimated diagnosticity effects.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.description: In Experiment 3 the congruent and incongruent conditions differed significantly in number of pre-target words (4.75 vs 5.23), a low-level confound for eye-movement measures. Although the authors added an interaction term to argue this did not matter, the conditions were not matched a priori on this dimension, and the post-hoc check relies on a non-significant interaction (a null) rather than true matching.
issues.quote: the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05)

issues.description: Hsound is computed using only the single 'most frequent pronunciation' of each suffix, while the comparison aims to show spelling carries more category information than sound. Collapsing each suffix to one pronunciation and restricting the entropy computation to words already containing that suffix spelling/sound does not properly capture how well a spoken sound sequence (which spans multiple spellings) predicts category, weakening the validity of the Hspelling vs Hsound comparison.
issues.quote: we calculated Hsound to provide an estimate of the prediction precision from the most frequent pronunciation of the suffix

issues.description: Specificity is glossed as 'probability of a cue given a category,' but it is actually defined as the probability of a particular spelling given a category AND a specific word-final sound sequence. This simplification conflates a conditional-on-sound quantity with a simple P(cue|category), which could mislead readers about what the construct measures and how it relates to cue validity.
issues.quote: needs to be expressed through the combination of diagnosticity and specificity (probability of a cue given a category).

issues.description: The non-suffix ending categories are reported as 88% noun and 'remaining 11%' verb (which sums to 99%), and then two adjective endings are mentioned separately. The loose use of 'remaining' and non-summing percentages is internally inconsistent and indicates imprecise reporting of the distributional comparison.
issues.quote: The majority of non-suffix endings are indicative of the noun category (88%), with the remaining 11% pointing to verbs.

issues.description: Interaction and main-effect terms were added to improve model fit, and a convergence warning was resolved by refitting with a different optimizer and declaring the warning a 'false positive.' Adding terms to improve fit and switching optimizers after warnings are researcher degrees of freedom that, without pre-registration, can bias toward detecting the predicted graded effects.
issues.quote: The original model produced a convergence warning when the variables were added. One way to assess if this warning is a false positive is to refit this model using a different optimisation procedure, such as “bobyqa” (Powell, 2009).

issues.description: The key entropy regression 'lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology, weights = suffix frequency)' is interpreted via its slope relative to 1, but it is not stated whether an intercept was included. Whether the intercept is estimated or suppressed materially changes the interpretation of the slope, and this detail is needed to evaluate and replicate the central spelling-vs-sound claim.
issues.quote: We then examined the slope of the regression equation lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology, weights = suffix frequency).
